query:
We are running a Bayesian-optimization alloy-design campaign on ALUMINIUM-based alloys for laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF). Powder is made in-house by ULTRASONIC ATOMIZATION of ~100 g charges (induction melting in a graphite crucible under argon, melt poured onto a vibrating sonotrode; induction module rated to ~1300 C). The current solute list is Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn. A collaborator suggested also including CESIUM (Cs), and cerium (Ce) is already included.

Please answer, with citations and quantitative values wherever the literature has them:

1. CESIUM in aluminium alloys. Is there ANY published use of Cs as an alloying or trace addition to Al alloys (for example as a eutectic-silicon modifier like Na, Sr, K, Rb; as a grain refiner; for precipitation strengthening; for corrosion; in Al-Mg or Al-Li alloys; Cs-containing brazing fluxes such as Cs-fluoroaluminates contaminating the alloy)? What does the Al-Cs binary phase diagram look like (solid solubility of Cs in Al, intermetallic compounds, liquid miscibility gap)? What are the physical constraints on charging Cs into molten aluminium at 700-1000 C under argon: Cs melts at 28 C and boils at 671 C, so what retention/recovery is realistic in an open crucible and during atomization, and what are the safety hazards (pyrophoric, water-reactive)? In what feedstock forms could Cs be dosed (metal in ampoules, Cs compounds such as CsF, Cs2CO3, Cs-aluminate flux, Al-Cs master alloys)? Based on all of this, what lower and upper bounds (in wt.%) would be defensible for Cs in an LPBF Al-alloy design space, or is the evidence that Cs is not a viable alloying element and the suggestion was more likely Ce, Ca, Sr or another element?

2. CERIUM in aluminium alloys for LPBF: what wt.% ranges have been used in published LPBF or rapid-solidification Al-Ce, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Ce-Ni, Al-Ce-Mn and Al-Ce-Sc-Zr alloys; where is the Al-Al11Ce3 eutectic and where does primary Al11Ce3 appear at rapid-solidification cooling rates; what are hot-cracking, printability and evaporation constraints; and what lower and upper bounds (wt.%) would you recommend for a design-of-experiments / Bayesian-optimization campaign? Also note how Ce is normally charged (Ce metal, Al-10Ce / Al-20Ce master alloy, mischmetal) and any oxidation or purity issues with each form.

Please state clearly where evidence is missing.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Abstract:
A part of radiocesium emitted during the Fukushima nuclear accident was incorporated in glassy water-resistant microparticles, called Type-A particles, which are spherical with ~ 0.1 to 10 µm diameter and ~ 10–2 to 102 Bq cesium-137 (137Cs) radioactivity; they were emitted from Unit 2 or 3 of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant. Meanwhile, Type-B particles, having various shapes, 50–400 µm diameter, and 101–104 Bq 137Cs radioactivity, were emitted from Unit 1. The chemical properties of these radioactive particles have been reported in detail, but previous studies investigated only a small number of particles, especially Type-B particles. We tried to understand radioactive particles systematically by analyzing a large number of particles. Micro-X-ray computed tomography combined with X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed the presence of many voids and iron-rich part within Type-B particles. The 137Cs concentration (Bq mm–3) of Type-A particles was ~ 10,000 times higher than that of Type-B particles. Among the Type-B particles, the spherical ones had higher concentration of volatile elements than the non-spherical ones. These differences suggested that Type-A particles were formed through gas condensation, whereas Type-B particles were formed through melt solidification. These findings might contribute to the safe decommissioning of reactors and environmental impact assessment.

Abstract:
<jats:p>As a new alloy manufacturing method that can break through the limitations of molds to manufacture fine parts, laser powder bed fusion has recently become a common process for producing aluminum alloys. In the fields of aerospace or automotive, aluminum alloys with both good printability and good mechanical performance in high-temperature conditions are greatly demanded, and the Al-Ce alloy is one of the alloys with significant potential. Therefore, systematic research on the additive manufacturing of Al-Ce alloys is still being explored. Herein, we review the recent progress and current status of laser powder bed fusion-produced Al-Ce alloys, giving our opinions on the development of this alloy system. Element composition, alloy powders, laser powder bed fusion parameters, microstructures, and mechanical properties at room temperature and high temperatures are summarized. The choice of alloying strategies is crucial for a specific mechanical improvement of the Al-Ce alloys. Finally, the details of the Al-Ce alloys manufactured via laser powder bed fusion are presented.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Aluminum (Al) and its alloys are the second most used materials spanning industrial applications in automotive, aircraft and aerospace industries. To comply with the industrial demand for high-performance aluminum alloys with superb mechanical properties, one promising approach is reinforcement with ceramic particulates. Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) of Al alloy powders provides vast freedom in design and allows fabrication of aluminum matrix composites with significant grain refinement and textureless microstructure. This review paper evaluates the trends in in situ and ex situ reinforcement of aluminum alloys by ceramic particulates, while analyzing their effect on the material properties and process parameters. The current research efforts are mainly directed toward additives for grain refinement to improve the mechanical performance of the printed parts. Reinforcing additives has been demonstrated as a promising perspective for the industrialization of Al-based composites produced via laser powder-bed fusion technique. In this review, attention is mainly paid to borides (TiB2, LaB6, CaB6), carbides (TiC, SiC), nitrides (TiN, Si3N4, BN, AlN), hybrid additives and their effect on the densification, grain refinement and mechanical behavior of the LPBF-produced composites.

Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Al-Ce and Al-Ce-Cr Cast Alloys: Effects of Cr and Solidification Conditions Valid Text Names: 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 1-6', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 6-11', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 11-15', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 15-22', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 22-27', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 27-32', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 32-35', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 35-36' BibTex: @misc{junior2026microstructureandmechanical, author = "Júnior, Gueber Elias Mendes Santos and Oliveira, Leonardo Carvalho and Silva, Argos Soares and Leal, Jaderson Rodrigo Silva and Barros, André Santos and Xavier, Marcella Gautê Cavalcante and Spinelli, José Eduardo", title = "Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Al-Ce and Al-Ce-Cr Cast Alloys: Effects of Cr and Solidification Conditions", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Sep", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10918756/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10918756/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Lightweight Al alloys capable of retaining mechanical performance at elevated temperatures are increasingly relevant for transportation and structural applications. Al-Ce alloys are particularly attractive because of their good castability and thermally stable Ce-containing intermetallics. However, how Cr addition modifies phase formation and mechanical behavior under rapid solidification remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the processing–microstructure–property relationships of Al–13Ce and Al–10Ce–1Cr (wt%) alloys produced by centrifugal solidification (CS), with directional solidification (DS) used for comparison. CS was performed using a stepped Cu mold with bulk diameters of 5–11 mm, and the resulting alloys were characterized by SEM/EDS, XRD, Vickers microhardness, and compression testing. CS produced markedly refined microstructures, with dendritic spacings of approximately 4.0–5.4 µm. The Al–13Ce alloy exhibited a cellular-to-dendritic transition corresponding to samples having smaller diameters, whereas Al–10Ce–1Cr retained a dendritic morphology throughout all conditions. The Cr-containing alloy generally exhibited higher compressive and yield strengths, reaching 282 and 143 MPa, respectively, compared with 253 and 119 MPa for Al–13Ce in the same 11-mm CS condition. The Hollomon analysis revealed a higher strength coefficient (K) but lower strain-hardening exponent (n) for Al–10Ce–1Cr, indicating higher resistance to plastic flow but a reduced strain-hardening capacity, consistent with the presence of primary Al 20 CeCr 2 particles. Overall, the compressive response was governed not only by microstructural refinement but also by phase constitution, intermetallic distribution, and particle/matrix interactions, highlighting the combined roles of alloy chemistry and solidification route in tailoring Al-Ce-based alloys.

A combination of thermal analysis and metallography determined the coordinates of the eutectic point at 644.5 ± 0.6 °C and 10.6 wt.% Ce, clarifying the existing literature ambiguity. Despite the high entropy of melting of the Al11Ce3 phase, in hypoeutectic alloys the eutectic was dominated by the regular morphology of periodically arranged lamellae, typical for non-faceted systems. In the lamellar eutectic, however, the faceting of Al11Ce3 was identified at the atomic scale. In contrast, for hypereutectic compositions, the Al11Ce3 eutectic phase exhibited complex morphology, influenced by the proeutectic Al11Ce3 phase. The Al11Ce3 eutectic phase lost its coherency with Al; it was deduced that a partial coherency was present only at early stages of lamellae growth. The orientation relationships between the Al11Ce3 and Al in the eutectic structure, leading to partial coherency, were determined to be [0 0 1]Al ║ [1¯ 1 1]Al11Ce3 with (0 4 4¯)Al ║ (2¯ 0 0)Al11Ce3 and [0 1 1]Al ║ [3¯ 0 1]Al11Ce3 with (2¯ 0 0)Al ║ (0 6 0)Al11Ce3. The Al11Ce3 phase with a hardness of 350 HV and Al matrix having 35 HV in their eutectic arrangement formed in situ composite, with the former playing a role of reinforcement. However, the coarse and mostly incoherent Al11Ce3 eutectic phase provided limited strengthening and the Al–Ce alloy consisting of 100% eutectic reached at room temperature a yield stress of just about 70 MPa. Hence using rare earth elements to achieve this purpose minimizes the advantage of conventional casting as one of the most economical fabrication processes, an alternative way becomes mandatory. In this regard, the group of Al-Ce alloys is currently receiving attention as the most suitable high-temperature candidate among the other Al-alloys. These alloys are characterized by their stability at high temperatures. Moreover, Ce is the most abundant rare earth element, which is beneficial in economics. In the current review, the metallurgy of Al-Ce alloys and the methods used to modify their microstructures are discussed. Special attention is given to melt solidification under ultrasonic vibrations as an efficient method to control the shape and size of Al 11 Ce 3 intermetallic particles and hence enhance the mechanical properties of the alloys. Future trends and prospects of these promising alloys are also presented. Abstract:
The Controlled Atmosphere Brazing (CAB) process together with NOCOLOK (cid:114) ﬂux is associated with the occurrence of potassium ﬂuoroaluminate residue inside the cooler. Excess of this ﬂux residue is known to cause gelation of the coolant, which deteriorates the eﬃciency of the cooler. The ﬂux residue amount is most often measured via Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy (AAS), in accordance with DIN ISO 9964-3. This is a time-consuming measurement that requires the use of specialized equipment and costly solvents. The following article presents two innovative methods for ﬂux residue measurement after CAB process. They include Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and Reﬂected Light Microscopy (RLM) with Diﬀerential Interference Contrast (DIC) module. The accuracy of these methods has been compared to the reference AAS method to evaluate their potential as alternative, less expensive, and quicker measurement methods for determining the quantity of ﬂux residue.

Abstract:
Solid lubricants are described as solid materials of intentionally introduced or in situ formed on contact surfaces in relative motion for the purpose of lowering friction and wear and providing protection from damage. Solid lubricants and advanced self-lubricating materials are widely used in modern industries, especially in aerospace, aviation, automotive, metallurgy, materials forming, and machining industries, and have attracted great interest in lubrication applications under very severe circumstances such as elevated temperatures, heavy loads, ultrahigh vacuum, extreme radiation, strong oxidation, and chemical reactivity environments. Many efforts have been made to develop self-lubricating composites by a variety of material preparation techniques, which include powder metallurgy, physical/chemical vapor depositions, thermal spraying, electrodeposition, laser cladding, and additive manufacturing. Although several reviews on the development of high-temperature solid lubricants have been published, most of them only focus on a type of material, a specific process, or application. In this paper, a comprehensive review is provided to present the state-of-the-art progress in solid lubricants, self-lubricating composites/coatings, and their effective functions that can be used over a wide variety of environmental conditions, especially at elevated temperatures. The solid lubricants considered include representative soft metals, layered structure materials (e.g., graphite, hexagonal boron nitride, transition metallic dichalcogenides, MAX phase), chemically stable fluorides, binary or ternary metallic oxides, especially alkaline earth chromates, and sulfates, and synergistic effects from these solid lubricants. The excerpt describes binary and near-eutectic Al-Ce alloys for LPBF, with the binary eutectic composition located at approximately 10.6 wt% Ce and an eutectic temperature of 644.5 ± 0.6 °C (also cited as 642 °C in relation to Ce solubility). Ce has extremely low solubility in the aluminum matrix, reaching only about 0.005 wt% at the eutectic temperature, and rapidly solidified LPBF material primarily forms stable Al11Ce3. A representative binary Al-10Ce alloy processed by LPBF achieved approximately 222 MPa yield strength, 319 MPa ultimate tensile strength, and 10.8% elongation. Although binary Al-Ce alloys have only medium room-temperature mechanical properties because Al11Ce3 does not provide strong strengthening, they retain substantial strength at elevated temperature: more than 60% of room-temperature yield strength and more than 40% of tensile strength at 300 °C. Their low Ce solubility and diffusion coefficient provide notable thermal stability and resistance to coarsening. In terms of printability, near-eutectic Al-Ce compositions show high liquid-melt fluidity and a wide LPBF process-parameter range, enabling crack-free samples. For bismuth, the cited chemisorption trend is Na < K < Rb < Cs, implying cesium has the strongest adsorption among those four alkali metals in that system. It also does not provide concentrations, microstructural outcomes, mechanical-property effects, or a direct ranking of Na, Sr, Rb, K, and Cs in aluminum alloys.

Metallic materials typically experience significant strength degradation at elevated temperatures. Traditional strengthening methods, which rely on thermally stable particle dispersion, exhibit limited effectiveness owing to the challenges in suppressing thermally activated dislocation motion. The proposed transformative approach paves the way for designing next-generation heat-resistant alloys, unlocking new possibilities for additive manufacturing in high-temperature applications.

Abstract:
High-performance conductors are essential for economically and environmentally sustainable ways of electricity transfer in modern infrastructure, manufacturing and transportation, including electric vehicles. This report reviews the aluminum conductors, their fundamentals, classification and utilization markets, focusing on metallurgical characteristics of present commercial solutions and the strategy of future development directions. The inherent features of aluminum, both beneficial and detrimental, for electrical engineering are emphasized along with alloying concepts that provide the accelerated decomposition of matrix solid solution to minimize the electron scattering. Development activities are assessed of new generation of aluminum conductors that in addition to alloying utilize novel processing techniques such as ultra-fast crystallization, severe plastic deformation and complex thermomechanical treatments aiming at grain reduction to nanometer scale, crystallographic texture control and grain boundary engineering. Transition metals and rare earths are considered as the promising alloying candidates for high-strength conductors having superior thermal stability with extra importance given to immiscible systems of Al–Ce, Al–La and Al–Y along with multiply additions, combined to generate the synergy effects. The composites with cladding configuration and particulate reinforcement including via carbon-type strengtheners are discussed as the effective solutions of advanced conductors. A variety of strategies that aim at overcoming the strength–conductivity trade-off in conductor materials are presented throughout the report.

Abstract:
Aluminum alloys containing small amounts of cerium have been investigated to improve the grain refining, casting characteristics, and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. These additions were usually made at levels of 1% or less but did not produce appreciable improvements. Recent work has shown that additions between 4% and the approximate eutectic composition of 10% improve the high-temperature performance of aluminum alloys. Corrosion performance of aluminum alloys can also be improved through the addition of Ce. Traditional aluminum alloying elements such as magnesium and silicon can be used to control casting characteristics and thermal and physical properties. Cerium oxide is the predominate oxide in rare earth mining. Much of it is discarded after separation from the heavy rare earth oxides containing Nd and Dy. The beneficial use of Ce should reduce the cost of the more desirable rare earths. Results of using Ce as an addition to aluminum in mul-tiple manufacturing methods such as additive manufacturing, extrusion, and casting are explored. The results show significant strengthening and improved mechanical property retention at higher temperatures than in other aluminum alloys and, in some compositions, show complete recovery of mechanical properties at room temperature when exposed to elevated temperatures as high as 500°C for 1000 hours.

silicon morphologies were investigated, the range of compositions

temperature gradient at which the morphology of the eutectic

pure alloy was measured.

concentrations of various impurity elements on the eutectic

definitive experiments on the growth of silicon into solutions

## pqac-00000029

From text 'phillips2005reactivesandexplosives pages 1-3'.

LB Phillips and C CHMM. Reactives and explosives: avoiding the big bang. Unknown journal, 2005.

The excerpt identifies cesium as an alkali metal and an air-reactive chemical. Air-reactive materials may react violently or spontaneously with air, and the text states that most reactives are also pyrophoric; pyrophorics can spontaneously burst into flames upon contact with air, although the flame is not always visible. Therefore, the excerpt supports treating cesium as presenting a serious ignition and handling hazard in contact with air. The recommended controls are to purchase only the amount needed, minimize the quantity used in experiments, keep the container sealed until the material is required, and date it when opened. Cesium and other pyrophoric air reactives should be stored tightly under an inert atmosphere or an inert liquid, such as nitrogen, argon, low-moisture oil, or kerosene. Transfers should be conducted under an inert atmosphere or liquid and, when available, inside a glove box. The excerpt does not specifically classify cesium as water-reactive, nor does it provide cesium’s melting point or boiling point. It separately discusses water-reactive materials and lists lithium and sodium—not cesium—in its example table, so those properties and the water-reaction conclusion require another source.

E.L. comp. Stout. Safety considerations for handling plutonium, uranium, thorium, the alkali metals, zirconium, titanium, magnesium, and calcium. ArXiv, Sep 1958. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/4336976, doi:10.2172/4336976. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt groups cesium with the alkali metals—sodium, potassium, lithium, and rubidium—and describes their hazards collectively rather than providing cesium-specific data. The stated hazards include explosions or fires caused by contact with water, chlorinated hydrocarbons, or other reactive agents; fires caused by exposure to moist air; injury from contact with hot metal; and caustic burns from residues produced by metal-water reactions. Thus, the excerpt supports treating cesium as highly reactive with water and moisture, with possible violent fire or hydrogen-explosion hazards, but it does not explicitly use the term “pyrophoric” for cesium. Safe storage requires a dry, designated area, with water or steam pipes and automatic sprinklers eliminated where possible and sufficient heat used to prevent condensation. On a laboratory bench, alkali metals may be stored in friction-top metal cans beneath water-free hydrocarbons or mineral oil. Glass containers should generally be avoided or placed inside metal secondary containment. The excerpt also recommends protective clothing appropriate to the quantity and temperature, including gloves and face protection for larger or hotter systems. It does not provide cesium’s melting point or boiling point, so those values cannot be derived from this passage.

The excerpt shows that cesium (Cs/caesium) was tested successfully as a modifier for the bismuth–lead eutectic: only 0.3 wt% Cs produced complete modification. Thus, Cs was tested as a modifier for at least one eutectic system, but this excerpt does not establish that Cs modifies eutectic silicon specifically in Al–Si alloys. The discussion mentions Al–Si eutectic modification by a third element through strong adsorption on the faceted silicon phase, which depresses the growth temperature and changes the silicon morphology from growth-temperature-dependent forms toward fibrous growth. However, no cesium addition to Al–Si is identified here. The excerpt also provides no ranking of the alkali metals as eutectic modifiers. It mentions sodium-modified Bi–Sn and Bi–Tl alloys in the figure captions and cesium-modified Bi–Pb, but does not compare Na, Cs, or other alkali metals quantitatively or by effectiveness. Any definitive claim about Cs in Al–Si or an alkali-metal ranking would require information from other portions of the article or external sources.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser surface remelting (LSR) has emerged as an effective strategy to refine microstructures and enhance surface properties of aluminum alloys. However, its application remains limited to Al–Ce-based systems, particularly regarding microstructural coarsening evolution within the melt pool, and oxidation behavior at elevated temperatures. In this context, this study investigates the influence of the LSR parameters on the microstructural evolution, microhardness, and oxidation of the Al–13Ce and Al–10Ce–1Cr (wt.%) alloys. Directionally solidified substrates were processed using single-track and overlaid-track LSR under different heat inputs (1.7–10 J/mm), and the resulting melt pool morphologies and cellular microstructures were characterized by Scanning Electron Microscopy and Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Vickers microhardness measurements were performed on the remelted regions, while oxidation behavior was evaluated by mass gain analysis during isothermal exposure at 640, 680, and 700 °C for up to 96 h. The results show that decreasing heat input leads to progressively shallower melt pools and significant refinement of cellular spacing in both alloys, with the Cr-containing alloy consistently exhibiting finer microstructures due to partial Cr dilution and segregation during rapid solidification. Laser-induced refinement resulted in an increase in microhardness, reaching values approximately three times higher than those of the as-cast microstructures. Although Cr addition refined the cellular microstructure after LSR and was effective in limiting oxide-layer growth at lower temperatures (up to ~ 680 °C), this effect decreased at higher temperatures (700 °C). It was observed that oxidation depended on microstructure and temperature: under fully solid conditions (640 °C), Cr prevented mass gain by forming protective Cr- and Al-rich oxides, while at ≥ 680 °C eutectic melting caused oxide spallation and loss of protection.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing (AM) can fabricate, repair, and join near-net-shaped components for high-performance engineering applications, including biomedical, energy, and transport sectors. The broader adoption of DED remains constrained by the limited number of alloys available that can be reliably manufactured without imperfections, hence limiting mechanical properties. Here, we designed an Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe AM alloy that can achieve an ultra-fine microstructure (<5 μm), uniform distribution of intermetallics, low residual stress (<32 MPa), and superior mechanical properties in as-built DED components. Compared to DED AlSi10Mg in the as-built state using the same conditions, the yield increased by 70%, and the ultimate tensile strength by 50%. DED-AM involves rapid cooling and complex thermal conditions, which largely influence the property of the final components. Post-characterization cannot capture the time resolved thermal behavior, hence offer limited mechanism-based guide for alloy design. In this study, we develop a novel multimodal characterization methodology for correlative in situ X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and infrared imaging, enabling quantification of the in situ thermal-related behavior, including phase evolution, temperature distribution, and stress accumulation during DED. We elucidated key mechanisms driving the structure refinement and stress development in this alloy. The insights gained into the interplay between alloy composition, thermal-related behavior, and performance under specific AM conditions inform next-generation material design tailored for AM technologies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In this study, prospects of designing new Al–Ca–Cu–Mn (Zr) alloys for additive manufacturing (AM) were evaluated for the example of laser remelting of thin-sheet rolled products. The new as-cast alloys have a hypereutectic structure containing Al27Ca3Cu7 primary crystals and ultrafine eutectic particles of (Al,Cu)4Ca and Al27Ca3Cu7 phases in equilibrium with the aluminum solid solution. The solid solutions are additionally strengthened by alloying with Mn and micro additions of Zr, which contribute to the formation of coarsening-resistant phases without compromising the manufacturability of the alloys. Laser remelting, which simulates AM-typical solidification conditions, promotes the formation of a pseudoeutectic cellular structure without the occurrence of undesirable primary Al27Ca3Cu7. The size of the dendritic cells and eutectic particles is 10 times smaller (for solidification rates of ~200 K/s) than that of the as-cast state. This structure provides for a higher hardness of the laser-remelted alloy (96 HV) as compared to the as-cast alloy (85 HV). Data for the alloy after 350–400 °C long-term annealing for up to 100 h show that the hardness of the Al–Ca–Cu–Mn–Zr alloys declines relatively slowly by ~7.5% as compared to the Zr-free alloy, whose hardness decreases by ~22%. Thus, one can consider these alloys as a promising candidate for AM processes that require high thermal stability.</jats:p>

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):

info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

Use the tools to answer the question: We are running a Bayesian-optimization alloy-design campaign on ALUMINIUM-based alloys for laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF). Powder is made in-house by ULTRASONIC ATOMIZATION of ~100 g charges (induction melting in a graphite crucible under argon, melt poured onto a vibrating sonotrode; induction module rated to ~1300 C). The current solute list is Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn. A collaborator suggested also including CESIUM (Cs), and cerium (Ce) is already included.

Please answer, with citations and quantitative values wherever the literature has them:

1. CESIUM in aluminium alloys. Is there ANY published use of Cs as an alloying or trace addition to Al alloys (for example as a eutectic-silicon modifier like Na, Sr, K, Rb; as a grain refiner; for precipitation strengthening; for corrosion; in Al-Mg or Al-Li alloys; Cs-containing brazing fluxes such as Cs-fluoroaluminates contaminating the alloy)? What does the Al-Cs binary phase diagram look like (solid solubility of Cs in Al, intermetallic compounds, liquid miscibility gap)? What are the physical constraints on charging Cs into molten aluminium at 700-1000 C under argon: Cs melts at 28 C and boils at 671 C, so what retention/recovery is realistic in an open crucible and during atomization, and what are the safety hazards (pyrophoric, water-reactive)? In what feedstock forms could Cs be dosed (metal in ampoules, Cs compounds such as CsF, Cs2CO3, Cs-aluminate flux, Al-Cs master alloys)? Based on all of this, what lower and upper bounds (in wt.%) would be defensible for Cs in an LPBF Al-alloy design space, or is the evidence that Cs is not a viable alloying element and the suggestion was more likely Ce, Ca, Sr or another element?

2. CERIUM in aluminium alloys for LPBF: what wt.% ranges have been used in published LPBF or rapid-solidification Al-Ce, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Ce-Ni, Al-Ce-Mn and Al-Ce-Sc-Zr alloys; where is the Al-Al11Ce3 eutectic and where does primary Al11Ce3 appear at rapid-solidification cooling rates; what are hot-cracking, printability and evaporation constraints; and what lower and upper bounds (wt.%) would you recommend for a design-of-experiments / Bayesian-optimization campaign? Also note how Ce is normally charged (Ce metal, Al-10Ce / Al-20Ce master alloy, mischmetal) and any oxidation or purity issues with each form.

Please state clearly where evidence is missing.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this detailed question about Cs and Ce in aluminum alloys for LPBF.

Abstract:
A part of radiocesium emitted during the Fukushima nuclear accident was incorporated in glassy water-resistant microparticles, called Type-A particles, which are spherical with ~ 0.1 to 10 µm diameter and ~ 10–2 to 102 Bq cesium-137 (137Cs) radioactivity; they were emitted from Unit 2 or 3 of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant. Meanwhile, Type-B particles, having various shapes, 50–400 µm diameter, and 101–104 Bq 137Cs radioactivity, were emitted from Unit 1. The chemical properties of these radioactive particles have been reported in detail, but previous studies investigated only a small number of particles, especially Type-B particles. We tried to understand radioactive particles systematically by analyzing a large number of particles. Micro-X-ray computed tomography combined with X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed the presence of many voids and iron-rich part within Type-B particles. The 137Cs concentration (Bq mm–3) of Type-A particles was ~ 10,000 times higher than that of Type-B particles. Among the Type-B particles, the spherical ones had higher concentration of volatile elements than the non-spherical ones. These differences suggested that Type-A particles were formed through gas condensation, whereas Type-B particles were formed through melt solidification. These findings might contribute to the safe decommissioning of reactors and environmental impact assessment.

Abstract:
<jats:p>As a new alloy manufacturing method that can break through the limitations of molds to manufacture fine parts, laser powder bed fusion has recently become a common process for producing aluminum alloys. In the fields of aerospace or automotive, aluminum alloys with both good printability and good mechanical performance in high-temperature conditions are greatly demanded, and the Al-Ce alloy is one of the alloys with significant potential. Therefore, systematic research on the additive manufacturing of Al-Ce alloys is still being explored. Herein, we review the recent progress and current status of laser powder bed fusion-produced Al-Ce alloys, giving our opinions on the development of this alloy system. Element composition, alloy powders, laser powder bed fusion parameters, microstructures, and mechanical properties at room temperature and high temperatures are summarized. The choice of alloying strategies is crucial for a specific mechanical improvement of the Al-Ce alloys. Finally, the details of the Al-Ce alloys manufactured via laser powder bed fusion are presented.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Aluminum (Al) and its alloys are the second most used materials spanning industrial applications in automotive, aircraft and aerospace industries. To comply with the industrial demand for high-performance aluminum alloys with superb mechanical properties, one promising approach is reinforcement with ceramic particulates. Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) of Al alloy powders provides vast freedom in design and allows fabrication of aluminum matrix composites with significant grain refinement and textureless microstructure. This review paper evaluates the trends in in situ and ex situ reinforcement of aluminum alloys by ceramic particulates, while analyzing their effect on the material properties and process parameters. The current research efforts are mainly directed toward additives for grain refinement to improve the mechanical performance of the printed parts. Reinforcing additives has been demonstrated as a promising perspective for the industrialization of Al-based composites produced via laser powder-bed fusion technique. In this review, attention is mainly paid to borides (TiB2, LaB6, CaB6), carbides (TiC, SiC), nitrides (TiN, Si3N4, BN, AlN), hybrid additives and their effect on the densification, grain refinement and mechanical behavior of the LPBF-produced composites.

Lightweight Al alloys capable of retaining mechanical performance at elevated temperatures are increasingly relevant for transportation and structural applications. Al-Ce alloys are particularly attractive because of their good castability and thermally stable Ce-containing intermetallics. However, how Cr addition modifies phase formation and mechanical behavior under rapid solidification remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the processing–microstructure–property relationships of Al–13Ce and Al–10Ce–1Cr (wt%) alloys produced by centrifugal solidification (CS), with directional solidification (DS) used for comparison. CS was performed using a stepped Cu mold with bulk diameters of 5–11 mm, and the resulting alloys were characterized by SEM/EDS, XRD, Vickers microhardness, and compression testing. CS produced markedly refined microstructures, with dendritic spacings of approximately 4.0–5.4 µm. The Al–13Ce alloy exhibited a cellular-to-dendritic transition corresponding to samples having smaller diameters, whereas Al–10Ce–1Cr retained a dendritic morphology throughout all conditions. The Cr-containing alloy generally exhibited higher compressive and yield strengths, reaching 282 and 143 MPa, respectively, compared with 253 and 119 MPa for Al–13Ce in the same 11-mm CS condition. The Hollomon analysis revealed a higher strength coefficient (K) but lower strain-hardening exponent (n) for Al–10Ce–1Cr, indicating higher resistance to plastic flow but a reduced strain-hardening capacity, consistent with the presence of primary Al 20 CeCr 2 particles. Overall, the compressive response was governed not only by microstructural refinement but also by phase constitution, intermetallic distribution, and particle/matrix interactions, highlighting the combined roles of alloy chemistry and solidification route in tailoring Al-Ce-based alloys.

A combination of thermal analysis and metallography determined the coordinates of the eutectic point at 644.5 ± 0.6 °C and 10.6 wt.% Ce, clarifying the existing literature ambiguity. Despite the high entropy of melting of the Al11Ce3 phase, in hypoeutectic alloys the eutectic was dominated by the regular morphology of periodically arranged lamellae, typical for non-faceted systems. In the lamellar eutectic, however, the faceting of Al11Ce3 was identified at the atomic scale.
